name: Flexibility and Efficiency of Use
description: Interfaces should work for novices while also enabling faster, higher-throughput use as expertise grows, often through shortcuts, customization, or accelerators. The key design problem is supporting the transition to expert use, not just adding power-user features and hoping they are discovered.
design_relevance_note: Shows up in keyboard shortcuts, command palettes, bulk actions, saved defaults, batch-edit flows, personalization, and progressive exposure of advanced controls for repeat users.
myth_risk_note: Real peer-reviewed evidence supports the general principle (expert-path efficiency and novice accommodation matter), consistent with this entry's existing partial backing, but the heuristic as a universal design law is not a single, cleanly validated principle -- this pass's evidence adds healthcare-IT-specific confirmation in the same direction.
prevalence_note: Canonical inside heuristic-evaluation and product-design practice, especially around shortcuts and power-user workflows, but less often cited as a standalone named 'law' than recognition/recall or minimalist design.

findings.description: Synthesizing the user-interface expertise literature, Cockburn et al. conclude that faster expert performance depends on more than simply providing accelerators: interfaces have to support the transition from novice to expert across repeated practice, switching to higher-performance methods, vocabulary extension, and better task mapping. Just adding power-user features is not enough; many expert components go underused unless that transition is deliberately supported.
findings.source_title: Supporting Novice to Expert Transitions in User Interfaces

applications.title: Adobe Photoshop reveals keyboard-shortcut accelerators via an unobtrusive hover overlay
applications.description: Nielsen Norman Group's deep-dive article on the 'flexibility and efficiency of use' usability heuristic describes how Adobe Photoshop shows a small overlay on hover indicating the keyboard-shortcut accelerator (such as 'W') for a given toolbar item. A novice user never has to notice or use the shortcut, but repeated incidental exposure to it during normal hover interactions supports learning it over time, letting the same interface serve both first-time and expert users without a mode switch.
applications.ethical_note: A discoverable-but-unobtrusive learning aid that helps users progress from novice to expert use at their own pace; no persuasive or manipulative dimension.

applications.title: Airtable pairs macro-style Automations with simple bulk-row checkboxes as two levels of accelerator
applications.description: Nielsen Norman Group's deep-dive article on the 'flexibility and efficiency of use' usability heuristic describes how Airtable offers Automations, a macro-style feature letting power users chain together multiple actions triggered automatically, alongside a simpler, more traditional row-checkbox mechanism for taking bulk actions (like coloring or filtering) on multiple table rows at once. Both are accelerators serving expert users, but they sit at different levels of setup effort and discoverability, illustrating how a single product can offer more than one route to the same efficiency gain.
applications.ethical_note: Accelerators that help expert users work faster without adding friction for novices; no persuasive or manipulative dimension.
